1.meaning: There is only one divine being, and nothing else shares in being God. Christians say God is one in essence, or nature, which means what God is. He is also three in Person, which means who God is: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. These are not two ways of counting the same thing, so there is no contradiction: there is one “what” and three “who.” This rules out belief in many gods. It also rules out thinking of the Father, the Son and the Spirit as three separate gods who work together like a team.
1.support: Deuteronomy 6:4 is Israel’s basic confession of faith: the LORD is One, so no other god stands beside Him to share His worship. In Isaiah 45:5, God Himself says there is no God but Him, which shuts out every rival, and Paul says the same in 1 Corinthians 8:4, showing that the first Christians held this belief too. These passages state plainly that God is one, but the further teaching that He is one in essence and three in Person is drawn from them together with other passages that show the Father, the Son and the Spirit each to be God.

2.meaning: God is not made of matter. He has no body, no size or shape, and no physical parts, so He cannot be seen with our eyes or confined to one place. This rules out thinking of God as a larger, stronger version of a human being. When the Bible speaks of God’s hand or His eyes, it uses pictures from our world to describe His real power and care. The Son did take a real human body in the Incarnation, but He added that human nature to Himself; the divine nature itself never became physical.
2.support: In John 4:24 Jesus states the teaching plainly: God is Spirit. So true worship is not tied to one holy mountain or building. In Luke 24:39 the risen Jesus shows what “spirit” means when He says that “a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” Read together, the two passages show that being Spirit means having no body. The body Jesus shows His disciples is the human body the Son took when He became man.

3.meaning: There was never a time when God did not exist, and there will never be a time when He stops existing. Nothing made Him or brought Him into being. He simply is, and everything else depends on Him. He is not merely very old, and He does not grow older, because time is something He created, not something that rules over Him; so He was never new or unfinished, and He will never wear out or pass away.
3.support: Psalm 90:2 looks back to before the mountains and the earth existed and says God was already there: “from everlasting to everlasting You are God.” That means there is no beginning behind Him and no end ahead of Him. In Revelation 1:8 the Lord calls Himself “the Alpha and the Omega,” the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, the One “who is and was and is to come,” so He stands at the start and the finish of all things; the further point that God is not bound by time is a conclusion drawn from passages like these together with the Bible’s teaching that He made all things.

4.meaning: God was never made, caused or brought into being by anyone or anything. He simply is, without beginning, and He does not depend on the world for anything, while everything else depends completely on Him. This rules out any idea that God came into being, grew out of the universe, or is one part of the created world, however great. It also means that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not created beings, but are fully the one uncreated God with the Father.
4.support: In Acts 17:24–25, God is the One who “made the world and everything in it,” and He is not served “as if He needed anything,” because He is the giver of “life and breath and everything else.” So He stands outside creation as its Maker, not as one more thing that needs to be kept alive. John 1:3 says that “without Him nothing was made that has been made,” which places the Word, the Son, on the side of the Maker rather than among the things made. The word “uncreated” does not appear in either passage. It is a conclusion drawn from these passages taken together.

5.meaning: God never becomes more or less than He is. He does not grow wiser, stronger or kinder over time, and He does not weaken, age or wear out. His goodness, faithfulness and love are the same today as they have always been, so His promises can be fully relied on. This does not mean God is cold or inactive: He truly acts in history, answers prayer and deals with people as they change, but He Himself stays the same in who He is.
5.support: In Malachi 3:6 the LORD says plainly, “I, the LORD, do not change,” and gives this as the reason Jacob’s descendants were not destroyed: because God stays faithful to His promises, His people are kept safe. In James 1:17 God is called the Father of the heavenly lights, “with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.” Unlike the sun and stars, which move and cast changing shadows, God is always the same. These verses speak directly about God not changing, and the full teaching that nothing in His divine nature ever changes is drawn from them together with what the Bible says about God being eternal.

6.meaning: God is not made of matter and has no body, so nothing about what He is could be seen by eyes, however sharp. This rules out picturing God as a very large or very bright creature, or thinking that any statue or image could show what He truly is. When the Bible tells of people “seeing” God, He was showing Himself through something visible, such as fire, a cloud or a vision, not letting them look on His very being. Even when the Son became man and could be seen, people saw His real human body, while His divine nature stayed beyond sight.
6.support: 1 Timothy 1:17 says it plainly, calling God “invisible” alongside “eternal” and “immortal.” John 1:18 adds that “No one has ever seen God,” yet the Son, “who is Himself God,” has made Him known, so we come to know the unseen God through the Son, not by sight. That God has no body at all is a conclusion drawn from these passages together with others, such as Jesus’ teaching that God is spirit.

7.meaning: There is no place where God is absent, from the room you are sitting in to the farthest star. God is not a huge being stretched across the universe, with a little of Him here and a little of Him there. Because He has no parts, the whole of God is present in every place at once. This does not mean that God is the same thing as the world, or that the world contains Him. He made all things and is distinct from them, yet no one and nothing is ever beyond His reach.
7.support: In Psalm 139:7–10 the writer imagines going up to the heavens, down to Sheol (the place of the dead), and out to the farthest sea, and each time he finds God already there: “Your right hand will hold me fast.” In Jeremiah 23:24 the LORD asks, “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?”, so no one can hide from Him. These passages show that there is no place without God. That He is present whole and undivided in every place is a conclusion drawn from them together with the Bible’s wider teaching about God’s oneness, not something either verse states in those words.

8.meaning: God is not built out of pieces that have been put together, and He cannot be split up. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three parts that add up to one God, like a pie cut into three slices. Each Person is the whole God. In the same way, God’s love, justice and power are not separate parts of Him. His love is simply God Himself loving, and His justice is God Himself being just, so no part of God can be lost, taken away, or set against another part.
8.support: In Deuteronomy 6:4, Israel is told that “the LORD is One.” This means there is only one God, not a group of gods or a collection of pieces. In John 10:30, Jesus says, “I and the Father are one,” yet He does not mean that He and the Father are two halves of God, for elsewhere the Bible shows that each is fully God. The Bible never uses the word “indivisible.” The church drew this conclusion from passages like these taken together: God is one, and the Father, the Son and the Spirit are each fully God, so God cannot be made of parts.

9.meaning: There are two different questions we can ask about God: what is He, and who is He? The answer to “what” is one: there is only one divine essence, one being that is God, and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each have all of it, not a share or a slice. The answer to “who” is three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct Persons, but They are not three beings or three gods standing side by side like three people in a room. So the Trinity is neither three gods joined together nor one God wearing three masks; it is one being, wholly possessed by three Persons.
9.support: In John 10:30 Jesus says, “I and the Father are one.” He speaks of two (“I and the Father”), so He does not claim to be the same Person as the Father, yet He says They are one, not merely in purpose but, as the rest of Scripture shows, in the very being of God. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son “the exact representation of His nature,” meaning the Son is distinct from the Father yet has the very same divine nature, not a lesser or separate one. Neither verse uses the word “essence”; the teaching is a conclusion drawn from passages like these together with the Bible’s clear teaching that there is only one God.

10.meaning: Calling God “Father” is more than a picture of His care for us. Within the one God, the Father is the Person who eternally begets the Son, while He Himself comes from no one. He has the whole divine essence, everything it means to be God, so He is eternal, all-powerful and all-knowing. Yet being the Father does not make Him more God than the Son or the Spirit, or older than Them, and it is not just a role God plays for a time: He is a real Person, distinct from the Son and the Spirit, and He has always been Father because the Son has always been with Him.
10.support: In John 6:27 Jesus speaks plainly of “God the Father,” and He shows that the Father is distinct from Himself, since it is the Father who places His seal of approval on the Son of Man. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul names the Father as the “one God … from whom all things came,” the source of everything that exists. In the same verse Paul calls Jesus the “one Lord … through whom all things came,” so the Father being God does not put the Son outside the one God; that the Son and the Spirit are also fully God is shown from other passages taken together.

11.meaning: To say the Son is God means He has the very same divine nature as the Father, not merely a similar or lesser one. Everything that makes God God belongs to the Son fully: He is eternal, all-powerful, and rightly worshipped. This rules out the idea that the Son is the first and greatest thing God made, or a half-divine being, or a second god beside the Father. He is still not the Father; He is a distinct Person, yet He shares the one being of God with the Father and the Holy Spirit.
11.support: In John 1:1 the Word already existed “in the beginning,” was “with God,” and “was God.” So He is distinct from the Father, yet He is truly God, and John goes on to show that this Word is Jesus. In John 20:28 Thomas calls the risen Jesus “My Lord and my God!” and Jesus accepts this rather than correcting him, while in Hebrews 1:8 God Himself speaks to the Son as “O God” and gives Him an everlasting throne.

12.meaning: The Holy Spirit is not a lesser being, a created messenger, or an impersonal power that God sends out, the way heat comes from a fire. He has the one divine essence fully, just as the Father and the Son do, so He is not a second or third God but the one true God. He is also a Person: He knows, acts, and can be lied to, which could never be said of a mere force. He is equal to the Father and the Son in glory, and He is to be worshipped and trusted in the same way.
12.support: In Acts 5:3–4, Peter first says Ananias lied “to the Holy Spirit” and then says he lied “to God,” speaking of the Spirit as God Himself. In 1 Corinthians 3:16, Paul calls believers “God’s temple” because “God’s Spirit dwells in you.” In 1 Corinthians 6:19, he calls the body “a temple of the Holy Spirit.” A temple is the house where God lives, so the Spirit living in us is God Himself living in us. No single verse here spells out the whole teaching, but taken together they show the Bible treating the Spirit as fully God.

13.meaning: In speaking of God, a “Person” is who someone is, not what someone is. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three real “Whos,” each able to love, speak and act, and each truly different from the other two. But They are not three separate beings or three Gods, because each Person is the whole of the one God and shares the one divine essence completely. This also rules out the idea that God is one Person who simply takes turns appearing as Father, then Son, then Spirit, like one actor wearing three masks.
13.support: In Matthew 3:16–17 all three appear at the same moment: the Son is coming up out of the water, the Spirit descends and rests on Him, and the Father speaks from heaven about “My beloved Son.” In John 14:16–17 Jesus asks the Father, and the Father gives “another Advocate,” the Spirit, so One asks, One gives, and One is sent; They cannot be the same Person. These passages show clearly that the three are distinct, while the truth that They are still one God comes from reading them alongside the many passages that teach there is only one God.

14.meaning: The Father and the Son are truly distinct from each other, and always have been. The Father is the One who begets, and the Son is the One who is begotten; these roles cannot be swapped or blurred together. This rules out the idea that God is a single Person who sometimes acts as the Father and at other times appears as the Son, like one actor changing masks. Yet being distinct does not mean being separate: the Father and the Son are not two Gods, because each has the one divine essence fully.
14.support: In John 17:1–5 Jesus lifts His eyes to heaven and prays to the Father, speaking to Him as “You” and asking for “the glory I had with You before the world existed.” No one truly prays to himself or shares glory “with” himself, and glory shared before creation shows that the Son was distinct from the Father before He became man, not only during His life on earth. In John 8:17–18 Jesus appeals to the rule that “the testimony of two men is valid” and counts Himself and the Father as two witnesses, which only works if They are two distinct Persons; that They are nonetheless one God is drawn from other passages read alongside these.

15.meaning: The Son and the Holy Spirit are both fully God, yet They are not one Person going by two names. Nor is the Spirit simply Jesus Himself, present in a new way after He returned to heaven. They are not told apart by being different kinds of God or by one being greater, but only by how each comes from the other Persons. The Son is begotten of the Father, while the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as from one source; these are two different ways of coming forth, both without beginning, so the Son and the Spirit share one divine life while each remains truly Himself.
15.support: In John 14:16 Jesus promises that the Father will give “another Advocate,” which shows that the Spirit is someone other than Jesus, who had been the disciples’ helper while He was with them. In John 15:26 Jesus says He will send the Spirit, and that the Spirit “will testify about Me”; the one who sends is not the one who is sent, and the one who testifies is not the one He testifies about, so these are two distinct Persons. That verse speaks of the Spirit proceeding from the Father, and the church’s teaching that He proceeds from the Son as well is drawn from reading it together with the rest of Scripture, which calls Him the Spirit of the Son and shows that all the Father has belongs to the Son too.

16.meaning: The Father and the Holy Spirit are the one God and share the one divine essence, but They are not the same Person. The Spirit is not the Father under another name, or the Father acting in a different way. The Father gives and sends, and the Spirit is given and sent. What tells Them apart is how They are related: the Father comes from no one, while the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son, as from one source. This is a difference of relation, not of rank, for the Spirit is fully and equally God with the Father.
16.support: In John 14:16–17 Jesus asks the Father, and the Father gives “another Advocate,” the Spirit of truth. The One who gives and the One who is given are clearly two Persons, not one Person seen in two ways. In John 14:26 the Father sends the Spirit “in My name,” which ties the Spirit’s coming to the Son as well. This sending happened in time and is not itself the Spirit’s eternal procession. But the church has drawn from these and other passages that the Spirit is sent in time from the Father and the Son because He eternally proceeds from Them.

17.meaning: God is not split into three pieces, with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each holding a share. God has no parts, so each Person has the whole of what God is: all His power, wisdom, holiness and life. This is why the Son and the Spirit are not lesser or partial gods, and why they are not three Gods either: there is only one divine essence, and each Person has all of it. We worship one God, and whether we pray to the Father, the Son or the Spirit, we are speaking to the whole God.
17.support: In Colossians 2:9, Paul says that “all the fullness of the Deity” dwells in Christ, not a part or a portion of it. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son “the exact representation of His nature,” which only someone who fully shares that nature could be. In Acts 5:3–4, Peter treats lying “to the Holy Spirit” as having “lied … to God,” and since Scripture takes for granted that the Father is God, these passages taken together, though no single verse says it of all three, lead to the teaching that each Person is wholly God.

18.meaning: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit have each existed forever, with no beginning. The Father did not exist alone for a while and then bring the Son and the Spirit into being. This rules out the idea that the Son or the Spirit was created, or is a later and lesser being. When the Bible calls the Son “begotten” of the Father, or says the Spirit comes from the Father, it describes an eternal relationship, not a starting point in time. The Father has always been Father, and so He has always had His Son, and the Spirit has always been with Them both.
18.support: In John 1:1–3 the Word, who is the Son, already “was” in the beginning. All things were made through Him, so He cannot be one of the things that were made. In John 17:5 Jesus speaks of the glory He shared with the Father “before the world existed,” and in Hebrews 9:14 the Spirit is called “the eternal Spirit.” No single verse states that all three are coeternal. The teaching is drawn from these passages together, alongside the Bible’s steady witness that God Himself is without beginning.

19.meaning: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not ranked as greater and lesser Gods. Each Person has the whole of the one divine essence, so each is equally almighty, equally holy, equally glorious and equally worthy of our worship. This rules out any idea that the Son is a lower, created god or that the Spirit is merely a power or force. The Persons are told apart only by how They are related to one another, not by any difference in rank or in how much They are God, and when the Son became man and obeyed the Father, He did not become any less God.
19.support: In John 5:23, Jesus says all should honour the Son “just as they honor the Father.” The honour owed to God alone may not be given to anyone less than God, so the Son must be God in the same full way as the Father. Philippians 2:6 says that the Son was “existing in the form of God” and already had “equality with God” before He humbled Himself, while Matthew 28:19 places the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit side by side under one divine name, with no hint that any is lower than the others; taken together with the rest of Scripture, these passages lead to the conclusion that all three Persons are fully equal.

20.meaning: God is not one Person who takes turns appearing as the Father, then as the Son, then as the Spirit, the way one actor might play three parts or one man might be a father, a son and a worker. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly distinct from one another, always and all at the same time, and They really know, love and speak to one another. Yet They are not three Gods, because each Person is the whole one God. There are no more and no fewer than three: the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Spirit who proceeds.
20.support: In Matthew 28:19 Jesus speaks of one “name,” yet lists the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit side by side, each named in turn as distinct from the others. In 2 Corinthians 13:14 Paul likewise names all three together, and each gives something to the church: grace, love and fellowship. Neither verse says in so many words that there are exactly three Persons. That is a conclusion drawn from passages like these together with the wider witness of the Bible, such as the Son praying to the Father and promising to send the Spirit, which shows Them as real Persons relating to one another, not one Person changing roles.

21.meaning: Perichoresis is a Greek word for the way the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit live in one another. Each Person is wholly in the other two, not partly, and They share one divine life, so where One is, the Others are too; They have never been apart and never could be. Yet They do not blend into a single Person: the Father is still the Father, the Son is still the Son, and the Spirit is still the Spirit. This also rules out picturing Them as three separate beings who merely work well together, like close friends, because Their unity is far deeper: They are one God.
21.support: In John 14:10–11 Jesus says twice that He is in the Father and the Father is in Him. He shows that this is real: the Father dwells in Him and does His works through Him, yet Jesus still speaks of the Father as distinct from Himself. In John 17:21 He prays, “You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You,” again naming two Persons who dwell in each other without becoming one Person, and He asks that believers may also be in Them, which happens by grace and does not make us God. These passages speak of the Father and the Son, so the teaching that the Spirit shares this indwelling is a conclusion drawn from the wider Bible witness that the Spirit is fully God, one with the Father and the Son.

22.meaning: God did not become Father at some point, such as when He made the world or when Jesus was born in Bethlehem. He has always been Father, because the Son has always been His Son; there was never a time when the Father was without the Son. Being Father is not a job God took on, a title He wears, or a mask He uses for a season. It is who this Person truly and eternally is, and this rules out the idea that the one God simply plays different roles one after another, or that the Son came into being later.
22.support: In John 17:5, Jesus prays to the Father about the glory He shared “with You before the world existed,” so the Father and the Son were already together before anything was created. In John 17:24, Jesus says the Father “loved Me before the foundation of the world,” which shows a real love between Father and Son that is older than creation itself. These verses do not use the words “eternally Father.” But taken together with the Bible’s wider teaching that the Son has always existed, they lead to this conclusion: since the Son has always been the Son, the Father has always been the Father.

23.meaning: To say the Son is begotten means He comes from the Father by sharing the Father’s own nature, not by being made. There is a real difference here: what is begotten is the same kind as the one who begets it, while what is created is of a different and lesser kind, as a house is different from the builder who made it. So the Son is not a creature but fully God, just as the Father is, and this begetting has no beginning: there was never a time when the Son did not exist, and nothing bodily is involved, unlike human parents having a child. Because the Father gives the Son the whole of the one divine essence, God is not divided and no second God appears; the Father and the Son are one God.
23.support: In John 1:14 and 1:18 Jesus is called the “one and only Son from the Father,” and verse 18 adds that this Son “is Himself God”: He comes from the Father, yet He is God, not something God made. In John 5:26 the Father has “granted the Son to have life in Himself,” so the Son’s life comes from the Father, yet it is life in Himself, just as the Father’s is, not borrowed life like a creature’s. That this begetting is eternal is not stated in any one verse; it is a conclusion drawn from these passages together with others that show the Son was already with God in the beginning, before anything was made.

24.meaning: “Procession” is the word for the way the Holy Spirit eternally comes from God. It differs from the Son’s being begotten. The Son comes from the Father alone, while the Spirit comes from the Father and the Son together, as from one source, not two. The Son has this from the Father, because the Father gives Him everything that is His, including being the source of the Spirit. None of this means the Spirit had a beginning or is less than the Father and the Son: He receives the whole divine nature and is fully God, and His eternal procession is not the same as His being sent at Pentecost.
24.support: In John 15:26 Jesus says the Spirit “proceeds from the Father,” yet He also says that He Himself will send the Spirit, and Galatians 4:6 calls Him “the Spirit of His Son.” In John 16:14–15 the Spirit takes from what is the Son’s, and Jesus gives the reason: “Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.” So what the Spirit receives from the Father, He receives from the Son as well. No single verse says all of this, but taken together these passages lead to the church’s teaching: the Spirit eternally comes forth from the Father and the Son as one source, and the Son has this from the Father.

25.meaning: “Relations of origin” means the ways the three Persons are related to one another by where each comes from, or does not come from. The Father comes from no one; the Son is begotten of the Father; and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as from one source. These relations are the only thing that makes the Father, the Son and the Spirit distinct, because in everything else, such as power, glory, wisdom and love, They share the one divine nature completely. So the Persons are not told apart by one being more divine, having a different kind of nature, holding a higher rank or existing first. This “origin” has no beginning in time, and it does not make the Son or the Spirit any less God.
25.support: In John 1:18 Jesus is called “the one and only Son,” who is “Himself God” and is “at the Father’s side.” He is fully God, yet distinct from the Father, and what marks Him out is that He is the Son of the Father. In John 15:26 the Spirit “proceeds from the Father” and is sent by the Son, so He too is marked out by where He comes from, not by being a lesser God. That the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well, and that these relations alone distinguish the Persons, is a conclusion drawn from these verses together with the rest of Scripture, which also calls Him the Spirit of the Son.

26.meaning: Before God made anything, the Father and the Son were already sharing a perfect love, so God did not need to create the world, or us, in order to have someone to love. This rules out the idea that God was lonely before creation, or that His love for the Son began when Jesus was born, baptised or raised from the dead. Because God does not change, this love has never grown, faded or started; it belongs to who God eternally is. It also shows why love is not just something God does now and then but lies at the heart of His very being, and the love He shows us flows out of this love He has always had within Himself.
26.support: In John 17:24, Jesus, praying to His Father, says the Father loved Him “before the foundation of the world,” that is, before anything was created. The verse itself places this love before creation. To say it had no beginning at all is a conclusion drawn when this verse is read together with the Bible’s wider teaching that the Son has always existed with the Father and that God never changes.

27.meaning: In the Bible, God’s glory is the shining fullness of who He is: His greatness, beauty and majesty. The Son did not receive this glory at some point, earn it, or borrow it. He has always shared it with the Father, because He has the same divine nature. This rules out any idea that the Son is a created being or a lesser God, since God gives His own glory to no creature. When the Son became man in the Incarnation, His glory was hidden behind His humble human life, but it was never lost.
27.support: In John 17:5, Jesus speaks of “the glory I had with You before the world existed,” so He existed before creation and already shared the Father’s glory then. He does not ask for something new, but for that same glory to be shown in His life as a man. That this sharing has no beginning and is a sharing as equals is a conclusion drawn from this verse together with the wider teaching of Scripture that only God has divine glory and that the Son is God.

28.meaning: A will is the power to choose and to want. It belongs to what God is, His one essence, not to each Person on His own. So the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not like three people who each have their own wishes and must agree on a plan; They share one divine will, though each Person wills in His own way, in keeping with how He is related to the Others. This rules out any idea of the Persons disagreeing, bargaining or overruling one another. It does not deny that the Son, when He became man, also took a real human will, which always freely followed the one divine will.
28.support: In John 5:19 Jesus says the Son can do nothing by Himself and does whatever the Father does, which shows that the Father and the Son never act from separate purposes but in one shared work. In John 10:30 Jesus says that He and the Father are one, pointing to a oneness deeper than simple agreement. Neither verse uses the words “one will”; the teaching is a conclusion drawn from these and other passages together, which show one God acting with one purpose, and from the truth that the Persons share one divine essence.

29.meaning: When God acts in the world, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit do not split the work into three separate jobs. They do one work together, because They are one God with one will and one power. Yet the Bible often links a particular work with one Person: creation with the Father, redemption with the Son, and making us holy with the Spirit. This is called appropriation, and it shows what is especially fitting to each Person without implying that the other two are absent or idle, so it rules out picturing the Trinity as a team that hands out separate tasks.
29.support: In John 5:19 Jesus says the Son “can do nothing by Himself” and that “whatever the Father does, the Son also does.” This is not because the Son is lesser, but because the Father and the Son never work apart; They share one work. In 1 Corinthians 12:4–6 Paul links gifts with the Spirit, ministries with the Lord Jesus, and ways of working with God the Father, yet insists that “the same God works all things in all people,” so each work is linked to one Person while none works alone; the full teaching is drawn from passages like these taken together rather than stated in one verse.

30.meaning: God’s being cannot be shared out in larger and smaller amounts. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each have the whole of the one divine essence, so each is fully God, with the same power, glory and majesty. The Son is begotten of the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. These relations only tell the Persons apart; they do not place one Person above another or make the Son and the Spirit lesser, junior gods. This rules out any idea that the Father is the “real” God while the Son and the Spirit are something less.
30.support: In John 5:23, Jesus says that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father. Since worship belongs to God alone, the Son could not rightly receive the same honour unless He were just as fully God. In Philippians 2:6, the Son is described as existing in the form of God, with equality with God already His own rather than something He had to reach for. These passages speak directly of the Son, so the full equality of the Spirit is a conclusion drawn from the wider teaching of Scripture taken together.

31.meaning: The Son did not begin to exist when He was sent. He was already the eternal Son, and the Father sent Him by having Him take on our human nature and be born as a man. Being sent does not make the Son lower than the Father or an unwilling servant: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit share one will, so the Son came as freely as the Father sent Him. This also rules out the idea that a loving Son had to win over an angry Father, since the love that saves us begins with the Father Himself.
31.support: In Galatians 4:4, God sends “His Son,” and that Son is then “born of a woman.” This shows that He was already the Son before His birth, and that He was sent by becoming man at the time God chose. John 3:17 gives the purpose of the sending: God sent His Son not to condemn the world but “to save the world through Him,” so the sending flows from the Father’s will to rescue. That the Son stays fully equal to the Father while being sent is not stated in these verses alone. It is drawn from them together with the rest of the Bible’s teaching about the Son.

32.meaning: After Jesus returned to the Father, the Holy Spirit was sent to live in His people, which came to pass at Pentecost. The Bible speaks of this sending as the work of both the Father and the Son. It is not one acting without the other but one shared act, as all of God’s works are. Being sent does not make the Spirit lesser, the way a servant is lower than his master: the Spirit is fully God, equal with the Father and the Son, and He comes willingly. This sending happened in time, so it is not the same as the Spirit’s eternal procession, though it shows us something true about who He is.
32.support: In John 14:26 Jesus says the Father will send the Spirit “in My name,” and in John 16:7 He says of the Spirit, “I will send Him to you.” John 15:26 brings the two together, for Jesus will send the Spirit “to you from the Father,” so the teaching comes from reading these passages side by side. The same verse also speaks of the Spirit “who proceeds from the Father,” which helps us tell His eternal coming forth apart from His being sent to us.

33.meaning: God the Father is beyond our sight and beyond our reach on our own. The Son can show us the Father perfectly because He is not a creature looking at God from outside: He shares the one divine essence with the Father and knows Him fully. In the Incarnation the Son became man, so in Jesus’ words, deeds and character we see exactly what the Father is like, with nothing hidden or different behind Him. This rules out the idea that Jesus was only a good teacher or prophet pointing toward God. It also rules out the idea that the Son simply is the Father under another name: They are distinct Persons, yet one God.
33.support: In John 1:18, John first says that no one has ever seen God. He then says that the Son, “who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side,” has made Him known, so the Son can reveal the Father because He is God and is closest to Him. In John 14:9, Jesus tells Philip that “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father,” so there is no need to look past Jesus to find the Father. Taken together, the two passages show that the Son is not the Father, yet He shows us the Father fully. That only makes sense if the Son and the Father are one God.

34.meaning: The Holy Spirit’s work is to show us who Jesus is. He opens our eyes to Christ’s glory, brings His words home to us, and draws us to trust and love Him. So the Spirit does not bring a different message of His own, or new teaching that goes beyond Christ or leaves Him aside. This does not make the Spirit lesser than the Son: He is fully God, equal in glory, and worshipped together with the Father and the Son. His way of working simply fits who He eternally is, the One who comes forth from the Father and gladly makes known what He receives.
34.support: In John 16:13–14, Jesus says that the Spirit “will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears,” and that “He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.” Here the Spirit’s message is plainly Christ’s own, and the aim of His speaking is to bring honour to Jesus. That the Spirit is still fully God, and not made lower by this role, is not stated in this passage but is drawn from other passages taken together.

35.meaning: When Jesus prays, He is not putting on a show or talking to Himself. He is a real Person speaking to another real Person, the Father, with genuine love and trust. This rules out the idea that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are only three masks or roles worn by one Person. It also does not make Them two Gods or make the Son a lesser God: the Son prays as the One who became man, and He is still one God with the Father, whom He knew and loved before the world began.
35.support: In John 17:1–5 Jesus speaks to the Father as “You,” calls Himself “Your Son,” and asks to be glorified “in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed,” which shows that this face-to-face relationship did not begin at His birth but was there from eternity. In Luke 22:42 Jesus prays, “not My will, but Yours be done.” Here His human will freely obeys the Father; this is not a quarrel inside God, who has one divine will. That the distinction between the Persons is eternal and not only something seen on earth is a conclusion drawn from passages like these read together, rather than spelled out in a single verse.

36.meaning: When the Father speaks to the Son, we see that Father and Son are truly distinct Persons who can address one another, love one another and answer one another. This rules out the idea that God is a single Person who merely takes on different roles, sometimes acting as Father and sometimes as Son, like one actor wearing different masks. One person cannot truly praise himself as his own beloved son or answer his own prayer from heaven. Yet this does not mean two Gods: the Father and the Son share the one divine being, and Their speaking shows a real relationship of love within the one God.
36.support: In Matthew 3:17, Jesus is standing in the Jordan when a voice from heaven calls Him “My beloved Son.” The one speaking and the one spoken about are clearly not the same Person. In John 12:28, Jesus prays, “Father, glorify Your name!” and a voice answers from heaven, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again,” a real exchange between two Persons. Neither passage uses the word “Person”; the teaching is drawn from scenes like these, read together with the Bible’s teaching that there is only one God.

37.meaning: The Bible speaks of the Holy Spirit as someone, not something. He acts in the ways only a person can: He speaks, He instructs, He makes choices and He has His own purposes. This rules out the idea that the Spirit is only God’s power or energy, like wind or electricity, which can be used but cannot know, love or decide anything. He is a divine Person, distinct from the Father and the Son, yet fully the one God together with Them.
37.support: In Acts 13:2 the Spirit speaks directly, saying “Set apart for Me” and “I have called them,” and gives a command as someone with His own purpose. In John 14:26 Jesus promises that the Spirit “will teach you all things” and remind the disciples of His words. In 1 Corinthians 12:11 the Spirit gives out gifts “as He determines,” which means He chooses. None of these verses uses the word “Person,” but together they show the Spirit speaking, teaching and deciding, things only a personal being can do.

38.meaning: When God made the world, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit did not each do a separate share of the work, the way builders might divide up a job. There is one God with one will and one power, so creating was a single act done by all three Persons together, though each acted in His own way: the Father made all things through the Son and by the Spirit. This rules out the idea that the Father alone is the real Maker while the Son and the Spirit are only His helpers or tools, and it means neither the Son nor the Spirit is among the things that were made. When Christians speak of creation as the Father’s work in a special way, they are not shutting the other two Persons out.
38.support: Genesis 1:1–2 says that God created the heavens and the earth, and in the same breath shows the Spirit of God hovering over the waters, present and at work. John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 add that all things were made through the Word, that is, the Son, and Colossians says they were made in Him and for Him as well; John says that nothing that was made came about without Him, so the Son stands on the Maker’s side, not among the things made. No single verse names all three Persons creating together, but read side by side these passages show the one God creating, with the Father, the Son and the Spirit all at work in that one act.

39.meaning: Saving us is not a task the three Persons divide up, as if each did a separate share. It is one work of the one God, done by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together. Yet each acts in His own way: the Father plans and sends, the Son comes and gives His life, and the Spirit brings that rescue home to us and changes us from within. This rules out the picture of a stern Father who must be won over by a kind Son, or a Spirit who only tidies up afterwards. The Father’s love is the source of the Son’s coming, and all three are equally for us.
39.support: Ephesians 1:3–14 moves through all three Persons in one long burst of praise. The Father “chose us in Him before the foundation of the world,” and in the Son “we have redemption through His blood.” Later in the same passage the Holy Spirit is the seal and pledge of all God has promised. 1 Peter 1:2 likewise names the three together in a single sentence about our salvation: the “foreknowledge of God the Father,” being “sanctified by the Spirit,” and the “sprinkling by His blood” of Jesus Christ. Neither passage says in so many words that the work is undivided. But the way both weave the three Persons into one saving purpose, read alongside the Bible’s teaching that God is one, leads the church to confess salvation as one work of the one God.

40.meaning: To be baptised “in the name” of someone means to be handed over to them, to belong to them and to come under their care. In baptism a believer is joined to the one true God, who is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from then on bears His name. Christians are not baptised into one Person while leaving the other two aside, nor into three different gods, nor into the Father with two lesser helpers. All three Persons are named together and equally, because all three are the one God the believer now belongs to.
40.support: In Matthew 28:19 Jesus tells His followers to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” He speaks of one name, not three names, yet He sets the Son and the Spirit right alongside the Father in the very act that marks a person’s entry into the Christian life, something no mere creature could share with God. This verse does not explain the whole teaching of the Trinity by itself, which is drawn from many passages together, but it shows clearly that Christian faith begins by being joined to all three Persons as the one God.

41.meaning: Of the three divine Persons, it was the Son alone who took a human body and soul and was born as Jesus. The Father did not become man, and neither did the Holy Spirit, so it is wrong to say that the Father was born in Bethlehem or died on the cross. All three Persons were at work in this one event: the Father sent the Son, the Spirit formed His human body in Mary’s womb, and the Son came. Yet only the Son was joined to a human nature, which shows that the Persons are truly distinct and are not just three masks worn by one God.
41.support: In John 1:14 it is the Word, called “the one and only Son from the Father,” who “became flesh,” and the Father is named as someone distinct from Him. In Galatians 4:4 God sends His Son, and it is the Son, not the sender, who is “born of a woman.” Neither verse uses the word “only,” but across the Bible the Son is always the one said to be born and to become man, never the Father or the Spirit, and the church draws this teaching from that steady pattern.

42.meaning: Becoming man was an adding, not a swapping. The Son took on a full human nature, but His divine nature was not reduced, set aside or changed into something else, because God is immutable. This rules out the idea that Jesus gave up some of His divine power or knowledge to fit into a human life, or that He was a blend, partly God and partly man. Even as a baby in Mary’s arms, the one Son was still wholly God while truly living a human life.
42.support: Colossians 2:9 says that “all the fullness of the Deity” dwells in Christ “in bodily form.” That is not a part of God but all that God is, present in the One who has a real human body, and Paul says it “dwells” even after Jesus rose and returned to heaven. Philippians 2:6–8 says the Son was “existing in the form of God” and then took “the form of a servant.” The emptying it describes is His taking that lowly place and humbling Himself even to death; the passage never says He stopped being God. Neither verse spells out the whole teaching alone, but read together, and with the rest of the Bible’s witness that Jesus is God, they show He added humanity without losing His deity.

43.meaning: A nature is what something is, and a Person is who someone is. In Jesus there is only one “who,” the eternal Son of God, but two “whats.” He has everything that makes God God, and everything that makes a man a man, including a real human body and soul. These two natures are not mixed into a blend that is neither fully God nor fully man, and His divine nature does not swallow up His human nature. Nor are they separated, as if Jesus were two people sharing one body, so whatever Jesus did or suffered, it was the one Son of God who did it.
43.support: In John 1:14 the Word, whom the same chapter calls God, “became flesh.” The one Son truly took on our humanity, yet the disciples still saw “the glory of the one and only Son from the Father,” so He did not stop being God. Hebrews 2:14–17 shows that His humanity was real and complete: He “shared in their humanity” and was “made like His brothers in every way,” so that He could die for us and serve as our high priest. Neither passage uses the words “nature” or “Person.” The teaching that the two natures are neither mixed nor separated is a conclusion drawn from passages like these together, which speak of one Jesus who is both fully God and fully man.

44.meaning: As God, the Son has no beginning. He has always existed with the Father and the Spirit, and nothing about His divine nature was ever made. But at a real moment in history, in Mary’s womb, He took to Himself a human body and soul, and these were created, just as every human body and soul is. This rules out two errors: that the Son Himself began to exist at Bethlehem, and that His humanity is somehow eternal or divine. The two natures stay distinct without being mixed, yet both belong to the one Person of the Son.
44.support: In John 1:1–3 the Word already “was” “in the beginning,” and “Through Him all things were made,” so He stands on the Maker’s side, not among the things that were made. In Luke 1:35 the Holy Spirit comes upon Mary and “the Holy One to be born” is spoken of, which shows a real human life with a beginning, brought about by God’s power. The teaching comes from reading these passages together: the same Son who is eternal as God also began a human life when He was conceived.

45.meaning: Only the Son became man, so only the Son had a human body that could suffer and die. The Father did not take on flesh, and neither did the Holy Spirit. This rules out the old mistaken idea that Father, Son and Spirit are just three roles or masks of one Person, as if the Father Himself was born, suffered and died. The Father was not distant from the cross: He sent the Son and was united with Him in the work of saving us. But the suffering and death belonged to the Son alone, and He bore them in His human nature, since God’s own nature cannot be wounded or die.
45.support: In 1 Peter 3:18, it is Christ who suffered and was “put to death in the body,” which places His death in His real human body, and He did this “to bring you to God.” In John 19:30, Jesus Himself bows His head and yields up His spirit, a true human death undergone by the Son made flesh. Neither verse says in so many words that the Father did not suffer. The teaching is a conclusion drawn from passages like these together with the wider witness of the Bible that only the Son became flesh, and that He was sent by the Father and prayed to Him.

46.meaning: When the Son became man, He added something to Himself; He did not lose or change anything He already was. He took on a full human nature, but His divine nature stayed exactly as it had always been: eternal, all-powerful and all-knowing. This rules out the idea that God turned into a man, or that the Son set aside His divinity for a time, or that God’s nature was mixed with ours to make something in between. It also means the Trinity itself did not change. There are still three Persons and one God, and the Son is as fully God in the manger and on the cross as He was before the world began.
46.support: In Hebrews 13:8 we read that “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever,” which says of the man Jesus what the Bible elsewhere says of God: that He does not change. In Philippians 2:6–8 Paul says the Son was “existing in the form of God” and then “emptied Himself” by “taking the form of a servant.” The emptying is explained by what He took on, not by anything He gave up, so He humbled Himself by adding our nature, not by losing His own. The teaching is a conclusion drawn from these passages together with the Bible’s wider teaching that God is unchanging, rather than something stated in a single verse.
